title: The grave

lines: THE SAME WORD, AT THE GRAVE.
cards: Two seas, loosed by their Lord, run up against each other and meet. Water against water. The Qur'an, in Surah ar-Rahman, says of them, in Pickthall's words: "There is a barrier between them. They encroach not."
The Arabic for that barrier is barzakh. Hold on to it, because the same word turns up somewhere much quieter. Not at the shoreline.

teach.h: SEND ME BACK. THE ANSWER IS NO.
teach.b: In Surah al-Mu'minun, someone at the point of death begs to be sent back, to do the good they left undone.

teach.h: A BARRIER UNTIL THE DAY OF RAISING.
teach.b: The answer is no, and then a phrase, Pickthall again: "and behind them is a barrier until the day when they are raised." Barzakh.
So the word that holds two seas apart also names the stretch between dying and rising: not this world any more, not yet the Day. The in-between.
It's also spoken of as the grave, al-qabr, though the barzakh is more than a hole in the ground. What happens there? The Qur'an says little in detail, and the hadith say more.

One in Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Ibn 'Umar, says that when a person dies, their place in the next life is shown to them morning and evening, and they are told: this is your place, until Allah raises you.
So the in-between is not empty waiting.
It is waiting with a view. Since it's part of the unseen, al-ghayb, scholars are careful to say the hadith describe it without explaining how. And notice what this does to a graveyard.
A hadith in Sahih Muslim has the Prophet, peace be upon him, going out at night to the graveyard of al-Baqi' in Medina, greeting the dead with peace and asking forgiveness for them.
He greets them because, in this teaching, the people in those graves are not gone.

teach.h: GREETING THE ONES ACROSS THE BARRIER.
teach.b: They are across a barrier: like the two seas, close, side by side, and kept apart.

how: Muslims visit graves to remember the hereafter, greet the dead with salam, and ask forgiveness for them; the time between death and the Day of Resurrection is called the barzakh, or the life of the grave.

o: the grave's two angels who question the dead after burial
a barrier; the in-between from death until the Day of rising
the narrow bridge over the fire crossed on the Day

p: a barrier until they are raised
where the dead were greeted with peace

s: in the Qur'an, the word barzakh is used only about death
in ar-Rahman it is the barrier between two seas.
a hadith in Bukhari says the dead are shown their place morning and evening
narrated by Ibn 'Umar: this is your place, until Allah raises you.
in al-Mu'minun, the one who asks to be sent back is given a second chance
the answer is no: behind them is a barrier until the day they are raised.

games.q: you're at the point of death in Surah al-Mu'minun, and you ask to be sent back to do the good you left undone. what's the answer?
o: no: behind them is a barrier until the day they are raised.
yes, but only for a day.
games.why: the request is refused, and the Qur'an names what lies ahead: a barzakh, a barrier, until the day of raising.

practice: Bring to mind one person who has died, someone you knew or someone whose name you only heard, and think of them not as gone but as across a barrier.
If you pray, greet them as the Prophet greeted the dead at al-Baqi', with peace, and ask forgiveness for them; if not, say their name once and wish them well.
And if missing someone is too heavy to carry alone, in the US call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Barzakh. A barrier; in Muslim teaching, the in-between of the grave, from death until the Day of rising. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a barrier, an isthmus, the thing between two things.

carryVoice: Your line: the in-between. Close, side by side, and kept apart, like the two seas. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.q: There is a barrier between them. They encroach not
and behind them is a barrier until the day when they are raised.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1379 (Ibn 'Umar: the dead are shown their place morning and evening)
Sahih Muslim 974 ('A'ishah: the Prophet at al-Baqi' at night)
